<reason>Both sides fought a genuinely tight, well-framed clash over the same crux: whether destroying physical enrichment infrastructure was worth losing verification given that the 60% stockpile survived. PRO built a strong frame (irrevocable concrete gains versus consent-dependent, revocable transparency; a closing window; bounded retaliation) and showed real epistemic discipline by refusing to invent a magnitude. But PRO's route depended on two points it never fully secured: how a "standing veto" operates over a program it can no longer locate, and how much closer or farther Iran actually is. CON pressed exactly those in Pressure Questions and PRO's answers ("the veto runs on belief, not omniscience"; "direction, not a number") handed CON usable material, which CON exploited with the Fordow example and the reframe that repeated follow-on strikes make the wider-war risk recurring rather than bounded — a point that speaks directly to the motion's "despite the risk" clause and was never squarely answered. Decisively, PRO's best offensive move — the alleged contradiction that CON both praises inspectors and concedes a warehouse sprint — was cleanly resolved by CON: the cameras guarded the watched feedstock, so a small cascade is useless without diversion, and diversion would have given days of warning plus a known target, i.e., an executable veto. CON also won the Osirak exchange with the more accurate account (the covert program was uncovered and ended by intrusive inspections, not the 1981 raid) and turned PRO's 60% evidence by tying that escalation to the collapse of verification. PRO's closing frame ("subscription Iran can cancel") was memorable, but CON's last word — cancellation was itself the alarm, and the strikes cancelled it while keeping none of the warning — flipped it. CON's two clipped turns are a real execution cost that narrows the margin, but its comparative ledger was the cleaner reason to vote.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>CON's answer to PRO's "your case tears itself in half" contradiction: inspectors were a notification service, and notification was the barrier, because the feedstock sat under seal at declared sites, so a warehouse cascade is inert without a detectable diversion. This preserved CON's "rubble for eyes" ledger and reversed PRO's revocability frame by showing the strikes moved the HEU off the books without Tehran ever breaking a seal.</best_rebuttal>
